cues.text: Hi, Rob. How’s the course going?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Oh, hi, Mia. Yeah, great. I can’t believe the first term’s nearly over.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: I saw your group’s performance last night at the student theatre. It was good.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Really? Yeah … but now we have to write a report on the whole thing, an in-depth analysis. I don’t know where to start. Like, I have to write about the role I played, the doctor, how I developed the character.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Well, what was your starting point?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Er … my grandfather was a doctor before he retired, and I just based it on him.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: OK, but how? Did you talk to him about it?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: He must have all sorts of stories, but he never says much about his work, even now. He has a sort of authority though.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: So how did you manage to capture that?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: I’d … I’d visualise what he must have been like in the past, when he was sitting in his consulting room listening to his patients.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: OK, so that’s what you explain in your report.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Then there’s the issue of atmosphere – so in the first scene we needed to know how boring life was in the doctor’s village in the 1950s, so when the curtain went up on the first scene in the waiting room, there was that long silence before anyone spoke. And then people kept saying the same thing over and over, like ‘Cold, isn’t it?’
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Yes, and everyone wore grey and brown, and just sat in a row.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Yes, all those details of the production.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: And I have to analyse how I functioned in the group – what I found out about myself. I know I was so frustrated at times, when we couldn’t agree.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Yes. So did one person emerge as the leader?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Sophia did. That was OK – she helped us work out exactly what to do, for the production. And that made me feel better, I suppose.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: When you understood what needed doing?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Yes. And Sophia did some research, too. That was useful in developing our approach.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Like what?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Well, she found these articles from the 1950s about how relationships between children and their parents, or between the public and people like bank managers or the police were shifting.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Interesting. And did you have any practical problems to overcome?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Well, in the final rehearsal everything was going fine until the last scene – what’s where the doctor’s first patient appears on stage on his own.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: The one in the wheelchair?
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Yes, and he had this really long speech, with the stage all dark except for one spotlight – and then that stuck somehow so it was shining on the wrong side of the stage … but anyway we got that fixed, thank goodness.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Yes, it was fine on the night.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: But while you’re here, Mia. I wanted to ask you about the year abroad option. Would you recommend doing that?
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Yes, definitely. It’s a fantastic chance to study in another country for a year.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: I think I’d like to do it, but it looks very competitive – there’s only a limited number of places.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Yes, so next year when you are in the second year of the course, you need to work really hard in all your theatre studies modules. Only students with good marks get places – you have to prove that you know your subject really well.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Right. So how did you choose where to go?
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Well, I decided I wanted a programme that would fit in with what I wanted to do after I graduate, so I looked for a university with emphasis on acting rather than directing for example. It depends on you. Then about six months before you go, you have to email the scheme coordinator with your top three choices. I had a friend who missed the deadline and didn’t get her first choice, so you do need to get a move on at that stage. You’ll find that certain places are very popular with everyone.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: And don’t you have to write a personal statement at that stage?
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: Yes.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Right. I’ll get some of the final year students to give me some tips … maybe see if I can read what they wrote.
cues.speaker: ROB

cues.text: I think that’s a very good idea. I don’t mind showing you what I did. And while you’re abroad don’t make the mistake I made. I got so involved I forgot all about making arrangements for when I came back here for the final year. Make sure you stay in touch so they know your choices for the optional modules. You don’t want to miss out doing your preferred specialisms.
cues.speaker: MIA

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: ROB
